passages.t: The nations left in the land
passages.happening:
The book's opening ends with a list. These are the nations the LORD left in the land ‘to test all the Israelites who had not known any of the wars in Canaan’ (verse 1), and to teach war to a generation that had never known it (verse 2). They are the five rulers of the Philistines, the Canaanites, the people of Sidon, and the Hivites of the mountains of Lebanon (verse 3).

“These nations were left to test the Israelites, to find out whether they would keep the commandments of the LORD, which He had given their fathers through Moses” (verse 4).

The answer comes at once. Israel lives among the peoples of the land (verse 5). “And they took the daughters of these people in marriage, gave their own daughters to their sons, and served their gods” (verse 6).
passages.hearers:
These verses close the long opening of the book. Chapter 2 said why the nations were left. This passage names them and shows what happened next.

The Philistines lived on the southern coast. Their five rulers governed five cities: Gaza, Ashkelon, Ashdod, Gath and Ekron. The Sidonians and the Hivites lived in the north. Israel was surrounded, and the test was real.

The list in verse 5 is the old list of the peoples of Canaan, the same names Moses and Joshua used. Israel was supposed to be different from them. Instead it settled among them.

Verse 6 names the problem, and it names it precisely: ‘and served their gods’. The law's warning against marrying the peoples of the land had always given its reason, that such marriages would turn Israel's children to other gods. In the ancient world a marriage joined two families and usually brought the gods of both into one house. The concern was worship, not birth. The same Old Testament welcomes Rahab, a Canaanite, and Ruth, a woman of Moab, when they turn to Israel's God, and both stand in the family line of King David.

These verses have been misused to forbid marriages between peoples and to rank one people above another. That is a false use of them. They give no ground for contempt for any people, and they lay down no rule about the origin of the person anyone marries.
passages.later:
The law had said exactly this: “Do not intermarry with them. Do not give your daughters to their sons or take their daughters for your sons, because they will turn your sons away from following Me to serve other gods” (Deuteronomy 7:3-4).

The New Testament keeps the concern about faith and drops any question of birth. Paul tells a widow that she is free to marry anyone she wishes, ‘as long as he belongs to the Lord’ (1 Corinthians 7:39).
passages.asks: Israel was not taken by force. It drifted, by marriage and friendship and habit, into serving gods it had been warned about. Ask which relationships and habits in your life draw your heart toward God, and which draw it away. And ask whether you have ever looked down on someone for where they came from, when God looks for the turning of the heart.

passages.happening:
“So the Israelites did evil in the sight of the LORD; they forgot the LORD their God and served the Baals and the Asherahs” (verse 7).

The LORD's anger burns, and he sells them into the hand of Cushan-rishathaim, king of Aram-naharaim, and they serve him eight years (verse 8).

“But when the Israelites cried out to the LORD, He raised up Othniel son of Caleb’s younger brother Kenaz as a deliverer to save them” (verse 9). “The Spirit of the LORD came upon him, and he became Israel’s judge and went out to war” (verse 10). The LORD gives the enemy king into his hand.

“So the land had rest for forty years, until Othniel son of Kenaz died” (verse 11).
passages.hearers:
This is the shortest story of a judge in the book, and the cleanest. It uses almost nothing but the words of the pattern laid out in chapter 2: Israel does evil, God's anger burns, an enemy rules, the people cry out, a deliverer is raised up, the Spirit comes, there is victory, and the land has rest. The book shows the pattern working as it should before it shows it breaking down.

‘Forgot’ in verse 7 is the key word. Israel did not argue its way out of faith. It forgot. The Asherahs were images or poles set up for the goddess Asherah, who was worshiped beside Baal.

Cushan-rishathaim is known from no other source. He is called king of Aram-naharaim, which means Aram of the two rivers, the land of upper Mesopotamia around the Euphrates, far to the northeast. His name means something like Cushan of double wickedness, which sounds like a mocking nickname given him by Israel. Because a king from so far away seems an odd enemy for a judge from the south, some scholars suggest the original name was Edom, which looks very like Aram in Hebrew writing. That is a guess, and the text does not settle it.

‘Cried out’ is a cry of pain more than a prayer of repentance. It is the cry Israel raised as slaves in Egypt. God hears it and acts.

Othniel was Caleb's nephew, the man who took the town of Debir and married Acsah in chapter 1. He belongs to the generation that remembered Joshua.

The Spirit of the LORD ‘came upon’ him. This is the first of several times Judges says so. In this book the Spirit comes on a person to give strength for a task of rescue. It is not a statement about that person's character, as the later judges will show.
passages.later:
The book of Joshua first tells how Othniel won his place: “So Othniel son of Caleb’s brother Kenaz captured the city, and Caleb gave his daughter Acsah to him in marriage” (Joshua 15:17).

The cry and the hearing go back to the exodus: “The Israelites groaned and cried out under their burden of slavery, and their cry for deliverance from bondage ascended to God. So God heard their groaning” (Exodus 2:23-24).

Samuel later remembered these years in the same words of forgetting: “But they forgot the LORD their God” (1 Samuel 12:9).
passages.asks: Israel served a foreign king for eight years before it cried out. Ask what you have put up with for a long time before bringing it to God, and why you waited. Ask what you are forgetting about God in the middle of ordinary life. And notice that the first judge is a man of faith from the generation before. Ask who in your life still remembers what God has done, and whether you have listened to them.

passages.t: Ehud and the king of Moab
passages.happening:
Israel does evil again, and the LORD gives Eglon, king of Moab, power over them. With the Ammonites and the Amalekites as allies, Eglon defeats Israel and takes the City of Palms. Israel serves him eighteen years (verses 12-14).

Israel cries out, and the LORD raises up Ehud, a left-handed man of the tribe of Benjamin. Israel sends him to carry its tribute to Eglon (verse 15). Ehud has made a short double-edged sword, and he straps it to his right thigh under his cloak (verse 16). He presents the tribute and sends the carriers away. Then, near the stone idols at Gilgal, he turns back. “I have a secret message for you, O king” (verse 19). The king sends his attendants out.

Eglon is sitting alone in his cool upper room. “I have a word from God for you,” Ehud says, and the king stands up (verse 20). Ehud reaches with his left hand, pulls the sword from his right thigh, and drives it into the king's belly, and he leaves it there (verses 21-22). He goes out, locking the doors of the upper room behind him (verse 23).

The servants come and find the doors locked. They think the king is relieving himself, and they wait a long time. At last they take the key and open the doors, and find their lord dead on the floor (verses 24-25).
passages.hearers:
Moab lay east of the Dead Sea. Eglon crossed the Jordan and took the City of Palms, which is Jericho or its oasis. That gave him the fords of the river and the land of Benjamin.

Paying tribute was how a subject people showed that it served an overlord. Goods such as grain, animals, silver or cloth were carried to the king's court by a group of men. It gave Ehud a reason to be there.

The Hebrew describes Ehud as restricted in his right hand, which most take to mean left-handed, perhaps trained to use the left. There is an irony in it. He came from the tribe of Benjamin, a name that means son of the right hand. And his sword was on his right thigh, where a guard checking a right-handed man would not look.

The idols near Gilgal were carved stones or images, perhaps a boundary marker. The upper room was a cool chamber built on a roof to catch the breeze, and it seems to have had its own toilet. That is why the servants waited outside.

The story is told with great skill, and with irony and some coarse humor at the expense of the king who had ruled Israel for eighteen years. Eglon's name sounds like the Hebrew word for a calf, and the storyteller paints him as a fattened animal. Ehud's ‘word from God’ is a play on words too: the Hebrew word can mean both a word and a thing. The first hearers, who had paid this king tribute, would have heard all of it. These notes do not dwell on it. A killing is still a killing.
passages.later:
The left hand of Benjamin is remembered later. In the war against Benjamin there were ‘700 select left-handers, each of whom could sling a stone at a hair without missing’ (Judges 20:16), and Saul's kinsmen of Benjamin were archers ‘using both the right and left hands to sling stones and shoot arrows’ (1 Chronicles 12:2).

Moab is not left as an enemy forever. In the days of the judges, a woman of Moab named Ruth came to Bethlehem and became the great-grandmother of King David: “He became the father of Jesse, the father of David” (Ruth 4:17).
passages.hard:
How can Scripture call Ehud's killing of Eglon, by a trick, God's deliverance?

The story is violent, and it turns on deceit. Many readers are uneasy with it, and they are right to read it slowly.

Readers have weighed it in three main ways. Some point out that Israel was under foreign occupation, and that Ehud acted as the leader of a war of liberation, where deceiving an enemy ruler was a normal part of conflict. Some note what the narrator does and does not say. He says that God raised up Ehud as a deliverer, but he does not say that the Spirit came on him or that God directed each act. On this reading the story reports what Ehud did without approving every means he used. Others read the whole book as growing more critical of its heroes, so that Ehud's cunning is a first step toward the more troubling judges who follow.

What the text clearly affirms is that God freed an oppressed people. It leaves the reader to weigh the means. These notes take no side among the readings.

Two things hold on any reading. This is a story about a war long ago, not a pattern for anyone today. It gives no one a warrant to deceive or kill anyone in God's name, and the New Testament forbids God's people to take vengeance into their own hands: “Do not avenge yourselves, beloved, but leave room for God’s wrath” (Romans 12:19).
passages.asks: Ehud's story is uncomfortable, and it should be. Ask what you feel when a story you are meant to cheer turns on deceit and killing, and say it honestly. Then ask a harder question. Where have you excused something you did because the cause seemed good? And ask whether you trust God to deal with wrongs done to you, or whether you have been planning to deal with them yourself.

passages.t: The fords of the Jordan, eighty years, and Shamgar
passages.happening:
While the servants wait, Ehud escapes, passes the idols, and reaches a place called Seirah (verse 26). There he blows the ram's horn through the hill country of Ephraim, and the Israelites come down with him (verse 27). “Follow me,” he told them, “for the LORD has delivered your enemies the Moabites into your hand” (verse 28).

They take the fords of the Jordan that lead to Moab and let no one cross. That day they strike down about ten thousand men of Moab, and none escapes (verses 28-29). “So Moab was subdued under the hand of Israel that day, and the land had rest for eighty years” (verse 30).

Then one verse tells of another deliverer. “After Ehud came Shamgar son of Anath. And he too saved Israel, striking down six hundred Philistines with an oxgoad” (verse 31).
passages.hearers:
The ram's horn, the shofar, was blown to call men to war. The fords were the shallow places where the Jordan could be crossed. Holding them cut off the Moabite army from home. Gideon's men will do the same against Midian (7:24), and the men of Gilead will do it, terribly, against their own brothers of Ephraim (12:5-6).

Ehud gives the credit to God: ‘the LORD has delivered your enemies’. The victory is told as God's work, done through a man's cunning.

The eighty years of rest are the longest in the book. Rest means peace in the land, an end of raids and of tribute.

Shamgar gets only one verse, a brief notice like those of the minor judges later in the book. The text tells nothing more about him. He fights the Philistines, who settled on the southern coast in the twelfth century BC. An oxgoad was a long wooden pole with a pointed metal tip, used to drive oxen. A farmer's tool became a weapon.

The ten thousand of verse 29 is one of the book's large numbers. Some scholars think the Hebrew word usually translated thousand can also mean a clan unit or a military contingent, and others read such figures as they stand. The note on chapter 12 says more.

The killing at the fords is war, told as war. Moab was the enemy of that day. Nothing here gives any reader cause to look down on the people of Moab, or on any people.
passages.later:
Deborah's song remembers Shamgar's time as dangerous: “In the days of Shamgar son of Anath, in the days of Jael, the highways were deserted and the travelers took the byways” (Judges 5:6).

Samuel later named Moab among the oppressors from whom God had rescued Israel in these years: “He sold them into the hand of Sisera the commander of the army of Hazor, and into the hands of the Philistines and the king of Moab, who fought against them” (1 Samuel 12:9).
passages.asks: Ehud told the people, ‘Follow me’, and he gave the victory to God before it was won. Ask whom you are following, and whether they point you to God or to themselves. And think of Shamgar, a man with one verse and a farmer's tool. Ask what ordinary thing in your hands God might use, if you would offer it.
